newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street stocks to focus on data at opening.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street stocks to focus on data at opening.

text.p: Wall Street stocks will take their cue Friday from U.S. economic data due before the market opens, with inflation figures the focus of attention.
"The markets are still in a nervous state and everything will be predicated on the two economic reports due out this morning," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
Retail sales and the Producer Price Index for March are due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, an hour before the stock market opens.
The consensus among economists polled by Reuters was that PPI would be unchanged from February. Excluding the volatile food and energy sectors, the index was expected to rise 0.1 percent.
PPI is one measure of inflation and could provide signs of whether the Federal Reserve is likely to raise interest rates again.
"If (PPI) comes in at expectations it should give us a strong opening, and that could carry through" the rest of the day, said Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood.
The consensus estimate for March retail sales is a 0.6 percent rise. Excluding autos, the rise is seen at 0.4 percent.
Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities, said Wall Street had already discounted the prospect of another interest rate increase in May. He sees a steady opening in stocks.
"The market has already baked in another Fed rise on May 20 and nothing is going to change that," he said.
In Tokyo the Nikkei Average closed up 361.23 points, or 2.07 percent, at 17,846.98.
In London the FTSE 100 index was up 5.2 points at 4318.4.
U.S. shares traded in London were steady in low volume.
The dollar moved in the low 126-yen range in Tokyo after falling close to 125.5 overnight. It was trading near session highs against the mark in Europe at 1.7240/53.
The U.S. Treasury 30-year bond was up 5/32 to yield 7.10 percent. The Standard & Poors 500 futures index was up 1.25 at 764.60.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column said high-definition television stocks are marking sharp upturns. The most-noticed stock is that of Harris Corp, which makes digital broadcast transmitters and antennas and also helps TV stations design and assemble digital studios.

The New York Times' Market Place column said Wall Street sees the auto industry as having reached a plateau. Despite recent bullish news, analysts are talking about the the Big Three auto makers mostly as a safe bet if the stock market nose-dives.
